items.prompt: In an 8-bit unsigned integer, what place value does bit position 5 represent when bit positions are numbered from 0 at the least significant bit?

feedback.reason: Bit position k contributes 2^k when it is set.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Binary is positional notation: counting from the right, positions 0, 1, 2, ... contribute 2^0, 2^1, 2^2, ... when their bit is one. Therefore position 5 contributes 2^5 = 32. The 8-bit width establishes that position 5 exists; unsigned interpretation means every set position contributes a nonnegative place value.

items.prompt: What unsigned decimal value is represented by the 8-bit pattern 10110010?

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Label the eight positions 7 through 0 from left to right. In 10110010, ones occur at positions 7, 5, 4 and 1. Their unsigned contributions are 2^7 = 128, 2^5 = 32, 2^4 = 16 and 2^1 = 2; summing them gives 128 + 32 + 16 + 2 = 178.

items.prompt: Under 8-bit two's-complement interpretation, what signed value is represented by 10110010?

feedback.reason: The same bit pattern can have different signed and unsigned interpretations.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

First read 10110010 as the unsigned positional sum 178. In an 8-bit two's-complement interpretation, a leading one marks the negative half of the 256 available patterns; subtract 2^8 = 256 from the unsigned value. Thus 178 - 256 = -78. Width matters because it determines both the sign position and subtraction modulus.

items.prompt: Which bit is the sign bit in an 8-bit two's-complement integer?

feedback.reason: The most significant bit is the sign bit in fixed-width two's complement.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Zero-based numbering gives an 8-bit word the positions 0, 1, ..., 7. Position 7 is the leftmost and most significant. In two's complement, that position distinguishes nonnegative patterns beginning with zero from negative patterns beginning with one, so it is called the sign bit.

items.prompt: Which bit positions are selected by the 8-bit mask 00101100?

feedback.reason: A mask selects the positions containing ones.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

A mask is a bit pattern whose ones mark selected positions. Label 00101100 from right to left as positions 0 through 7: the one digits occur at positions 2, 3 and 5. The zeros at positions 0, 1, 4, 6 and 7 mean those positions are not selected.

items.prompt: Using an 8-bit width-limited complement, what is the result of complementing 00001111?

options.text: An unlimited sequence of leading ones followed by 11110000.

feedback.reason: Width-limited complement flips each of the eight declared bits.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Bitwise complement swaps zero and one at every represented position. The question fixes exactly eight positions, so 00001111 becomes 11110000: the four high zeros turn to ones and the four low ones turn to zeros. No ninth or unlimited leading position belongs to the declared result.

items.prompt: The 8-bit pattern 11111111 is interpreted first as unsigned and then as signed two's complement. Which pair is correct?

feedback.reason: Bits do not carry signedness by themselves; the type interpretation supplies it.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

As unsigned, eight ones sum to 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255. Under eight-bit two's complement, the same leading-one pattern lies in the negative range and all ones is the encoding of -1. Stored bits are identical; the declared interpretation supplies the numeric meaning.

items.prompt: A 4-bit unsigned value 1101 is widened to 8 bits without changing its numeric value. Which representation is correct?

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The unsigned source 1101 equals 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. Widening adds four new high positions. Filling them with zeros contributes no new place value, yielding 00001101 and preserving 13. Moving existing bits or filling high positions with ones would change the numeric value.

items.prompt: A 4-bit two's-complement value 1101 is sign-extended to 8 bits. Which representation preserves its signed value?

feedback.reason: Signed widening repeats the source sign bit in the new high positions.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Four-bit 1101 has a leading sign bit and represents unsigned 13 minus 2^4, or -3. To widen without changing that negative value, repeat the source sign bit into every new high position, producing 11111101. Its unsigned value 253 minus 2^8 is again -3.

items.prompt: Which expression denotes a one-hot mask selecting zero-based bit position k when the value 1 can be shifted safely within the declared width?

options.text: A word with every bit set.

feedback.reason: A one-hot mask contains exactly one set bit at the selected position.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Start from a pattern with one only at position 0. A left shift by k moves that one to position k and inserts zeros below it, producing a one-hot selector with exactly one set bit. The expression is valid only when the operand type can represent position k and 0 ≤ k < its declared usable width.

items.prompt: Which statements about fixed-width two's-complement representation are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The same bits can have different signed and unsigned numeric interpretations.
A word of all ones represents -1 when interpreted as signed two's complement.
The most significant bit is the sign bit.
The numeric signed value is independent of the declared width.

feedback.reason: Two's complement is a fixed-width interpretation model.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

A two's-complement value is interpreted relative to a fixed width w: position w - 1 is the sign position, all ones encodes -1, and the same pattern can have a different unsigned meaning. Changing width moves the sign position and changes the subtraction modulus 2^w, so signed value is not independent of width.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe a bit mask? Select all that apply.

options.text: Set mask bits identify selected positions.
A mask may contain one or multiple set bits.
The semantic meaning of a selected position comes from the surrounding contract.
Every mask is inherently a signed negative number.

feedback.reason: A mask is a positional selection pattern whose meaning is contract-defined.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

A bit mask uses ones as selectors and zeros as nonselectors. It may choose one position or many. What position i means—feature i, permission i or element i—comes from the surrounding mapping contract, not from the numeric value of the word. Signedness changes numeric interpretation but not which physical positions contain ones.

items.prompt: Which operations or interpretations require an explicit width model to avoid ambiguity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Interpreting a negative two's-complement bit pattern.
AND of two explicitly written finite nonnegative low-bit patterns.

feedback.reason: Width-sensitive operations depend on where the word begins and ends.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

Complement must know how many positions to flip, negative two's-complement meaning must know which position is the sign bit, and truncation must know which positions lie above the target boundary. By contrast, AND of two fully displayed nonnegative finite patterns can be evaluated position by position without inventing unseen leading bits.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for interpreting a fixed-width unsigned bit pattern.

elements.text: Number positions from 0 at the least significant bit.
Map each set position k to 2^k.

feedback.reason: Unsigned interpretation is a positional sum.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

First fix the finite width and unsigned interpretation. Number positions from right to left beginning at zero, map each one to 2^k, then sum those contributions. Keeping the numbering step before arithmetic prevents accidentally reading the printed string left-to-right as positions 0 upward.

items: Write the pattern at its declared width and confirm unsigned interpretation.

For every one bit at position k, record the contribution 2^k.
Sum all recorded contributions.

blocks.title: Decision rule
blocks.text: For an ordering task, put the representation contract first. Only then interpret positions or values; reversing that order is how sign and off-by-one errors enter the reasoning.

items.prompt: Arrange the steps for interpreting an 8-bit two's-complement pattern whose most significant bit is one.

elements.text: Compute the unsigned value of the eight bits.
Observe that bit 7 is set, so signed interpretation is negative.

feedback.reason: For a fixed-width two's-complement word, negative signed value equals unsigned value minus 2^width.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

An 8-bit leading one marks the negative half of two's-complement patterns. Compute the ordinary unsigned positional sum U first, then subtract the full pattern count 2^8 = 256 to obtain the signed value U - 256. This sequence makes the sign decision and width-dependent modulus explicit.

items: Confirm the width is eight and the most significant bit is one.

Subtract 2^8 = 256.
Report U - 256 as the signed two's-complement value.

items.prompt: An algorithm inspects every bit of an arbitrary-precision nonnegative integer represented with w significant bits and uses only a counter. Select time and auxiliary-space complexity.
constraints: The representation width w may grow with the input.

feedback.reason: Bit operations are not automatically O(1) when integer width is part of the input.

blocks.text: How to reason it out

The algorithm explicitly visits each of the w significant bit positions, so it performs w·O(1) inspection work and takes O(w) time. It retains only a fixed-size counter and loop state rather than a second w-bit structure, so auxiliary space is O(1). A machine-word O(1) shortcut is invalid because w is an input-dependent width here.
